lessons.title: I/O stream basics
lessons.summary: Byte vs character streams, wrapping and closing.

blocks.text: `java.io` moves data as a **stream**: one value after another, from a source (file, keyboard, network) or to a destination.
There are two families, and the class name tells you which one you have:

items: Ends in **Stream** → bytes: `FileInputStream`, `BufferedOutputStream`, `ObjectInputStream`, `PrintStream`.
Ends in **Reader/Writer** → characters: `FileReader`, `BufferedWriter`, `PrintWriter`.
Use byte streams for binary data (images, serialized objects), character streams for text.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python picks the mode with one `open()` call: `'rb'` vs `'r'`. Java uses **different classes** for bytes and text, and the compiler won't let you mix them up.
A **low-level** stream connects directly to a source, such as a file. A **high-level** stream **wraps** another stream and adds features: buffering, lines, objects, formatting.

blocks.caption: High-level wrapping low-level of the same family

blocks.title: Families don't mix
blocks.text: `new BufferedReader(new FileInputStream(f))` does **not compile**: `BufferedReader` wants a `Reader`. To turn bytes into chars, use the bridge `InputStreamReader` (and `OutputStreamWriter` for output).

blocks.caption: bytes → InputStreamReader → chars

blocks.text: `InputStreamReader` is a `Reader` that takes an `InputStream`. You'll see it most often with the keyboard: `new InputStreamReader(System.in)`, because `System.in` is a byte stream.

blocks.title: Read the constructor
blocks.text: To decide if a wrapping compiles, ask: what type does this constructor take? `Buffered*Stream` and `Object*Stream` take a byte stream, `BufferedReader` takes a `Reader`, `BufferedWriter` takes a `Writer`.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `BufferedReader` wraps a `Reader` and `ObjectInputStream` wraps an `InputStream`: same family, so both compile. Option 2 and 3 mix families. Option 5 is backwards: `BufferedReader` has no `String` constructor, and `FileReader` has no `BufferedReader` constructor.

blocks.text: The basic `read()` method of both `InputStream` and `Reader` returns an `int`: the next byte (0–255) or char, or **-1 at the end** of the stream.

blocks.caption: The classic read loop

blocks.title: Why int, not byte?
blocks.text: A `byte` can't represent "no more data" separately from a real value. Returning `int` leaves room for -1. Exam code that stores the result in a `byte` or `char` without a cast does not compile.

steps.explanation: The file has 3 bytes: `a`, `b`, `c`. `read()` returns each, then -1, which ends the loop without being counted.

items: Buffered and other output streams keep data in memory. `flush()` pushes it to the destination.
`close()` flushes and then releases the file handle.
Closing the **outer** wrapper also closes the stream it wraps.
Use **try-with-resources**: every resource declared in `try (...)` is closed automatically, in **reverse** order of declaration, even if an exception is thrown.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Forgetting to close or flush a buffered writer means the data may never reach the file. Expect a question asking what a file contains after code that never closes its writer.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `BufferedWriter` stores "hello" in its buffer. Nothing calls `flush()` or `close()` before `Files.size`, so the file is still empty: **0** bytes.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it reads the first line of notes.txt and closes the reader automatically.
steps.explanation: Try-with-resources is `try (resource) { ... }`. `BufferedReader` needs a `Reader`, so the low-level stream is `FileReader`; `FileInputStream` is a byte stream and would not compile here.

steps.prompt: When a try-with-resources statement declares two resources, they are closed in the same order they were declared.
steps.explanation: Resources are closed in **reverse** order: the last one declared is closed first. That way a wrapper is closed before the stream it may depend on.
Like `InputStream.read()`, `Reader.read()` returns an `int`: the char value 0–65535, or -1 at end of stream. You cast to `char` to use it as a character.

lessons.title: Reading & writing text
lessons.summary: readLine, newLine, PrintWriter and append mode.

blocks.text: `BufferedReader` adds `readLine()`: it returns one line **without** the line break, or **null** at the end of the stream.

blocks.caption: Reading line by line

blocks.title: null vs -1
blocks.text: `read()` signals the end with **-1**. `readLine()` signals it with **null**. Mixing them up (`readLine() != -1`) does not compile: you can't compare a `String` with an `int`.

`mark(limit)` remembers the current position; `reset()` jumps back to it, as long as you read at most `limit` characters in between. `skip(n)` jumps forward. A `reset()` also undoes any `skip` after the mark.

blocks.caption: Read a, skip b c, read d, back to a

blocks.title: reset without mark
blocks.text: Calling `reset()` on a `BufferedReader` with no valid mark throws `IOException`. Not every stream supports marks: check `markSupported()`.

steps.explanation: `readLine()` returns `"a"`, `""` (the empty line between the two breaks) and `"b"`. Then it returns `null`. An empty line is still a line, so the count is **3**.

blocks.text: `BufferedWriter` adds `newLine()`, which writes the platform's line separator. `write(String)` writes exactly what you give it, with no line break.
`FileWriter` **overwrites** the file by default. Pass `true` as the second argument to **append** instead.

blocks.caption: Only the middle writer appends

blocks.title: Declared type matters
blocks.text: `newLine()` and `readLine()` exist only on `BufferedWriter` / `BufferedReader`. If the variable is declared as `Writer` or `Reader`, calling them does not compile, even when the object really is buffered.
`reader.transferTo(writer)` (Java 10) copies every remaining character and returns how many as a `long`. It doesn't flush or close either side.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that causes a compilation error.
steps.explanation: The declared type is `Writer`, and `Writer` has no `newLine()` method. The compiler only looks at the reference type. Declaring `BufferedWriter w` fixes it.

blocks.text: `PrintWriter` (characters) and `PrintStream` (bytes) add `print`, `println`, `printf` and `format`. `System.out` and `System.err` are `PrintStream`s.

items: Their print methods **never throw `IOException`**. Errors are recorded and can be checked with `checkError()`.
Their **constructors** that open a file can still throw `FileNotFoundException`.
`PrintWriter` can wrap a `Writer` **or** an `OutputStream`, or take a file name directly.
`printf` and `format` do the same thing: `%s` text, `%d` integer, `%.2f` decimal, `%n` line break.

blocks.caption: PrintWriter writing into a String

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: `printf("%s=%d", ...)` is like Python's `"%s=%d" % (...)`. Java's `%n` is the portable line break.

steps.prompt: `PrintWriter.println(String)` can throw an `IOException`, so calls to it must be inside a try/catch.
steps.explanation: Print methods of `PrintWriter` and `PrintStream` swallow I/O errors and set an internal flag instead; call `checkError()` to see it. That's why `System.out.println` never needs a try/catch.

`PrintWriter` is special: it has constructors for both `Writer` and `OutputStream`. `PrintStream` has no `Writer` constructor, `BufferedWriter` needs a `Writer`, and `FileWriter` has no stream constructor.

steps.prompt: Put the lines in order to print every line of a file, closing the reader automatically.
steps.explanation: Declare the resource in `try (...)`, declare the loop variable, then assign and test in one expression: `(line = r.readLine()) != null`.
The first writer creates the file with `a`. The second opens it in append mode (`true`) and adds `b`, so the file contains `ab`.

blocks.text: They are opened by the JVM. Don't close them yourself: once `System.out` is closed, later prints silently go nowhere.

blocks.caption: Reading a line from the keyboard with streams

blocks.title: out vs err
blocks.text: Both usually show up in the terminal, but they are separate streams. Redirecting output to a file (`> out.txt`) captures `System.out` only.
`System.console()` returns a `java.io.Console`, or **null** when there is no interactive console (for example in an IDE or when input is redirected). Always check for null.

items: `readLine()` / `readLine(fmt, args...)` return a `String`.
`readPassword()` returns a **`char[]`** and does not echo what you type.
`format` and `printf` print formatted text and return the `Console`.
`reader()` returns a `Reader`, `writer()` a `PrintWriter`.

blocks.title: Why char[]?
blocks.text: A `String` is immutable and may stay in memory (and the string pool) until garbage collection. A `char[]` can be wiped right after use with `Arrays.fill`. Expect this reason on the exam.

steps.prompt: What is the return type of `Console.readPassword()`?
steps.explanation: It returns `char[]` so the program can overwrite the password in memory as soon as it's done with it.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about `java.io.Console` are true? Choose two.
options: `new Console()` creates a console for the current process.
`readLine(String fmt, Object... args)` prints a prompt and reads a line.
steps.explanation: There's no public constructor; you get the Console from `System.console()`, which may be null. `readLine` can take a format prompt. `readPassword` hides the input, and `format`/`printf` return the `Console` itself so calls can be chained.

steps.prompt: A program that calls `System.console().readLine()` always works, because every Java program has a console.
steps.explanation: When no interactive console is attached (IDE run, background job, redirected input), `System.console()` returns null, and calling `readLine()` on it throws a `NullPointerException`.

blocks.text: `java.util.Scanner` reads tokens from `System.in`, a `String` or a file: `nextInt()`, `nextDouble()`, `next()` (one word), `nextLine()` (rest of the line), plus `hasNext...()` checks.

blocks.caption: Scanner over a String

blocks.title: nextInt() then nextLine()
blocks.text: `nextInt()` stops right after the number. The following `nextLine()` returns the **rest of that same line** (here `" days"`, or `""` if the number ended the line), not the next line.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `nextInt()` reads `5` and stops before the line break. `nextLine()` then returns what's left of line 1: an empty string.

steps.prompt: Complete the code to read one line from the keyboard using streams.
steps.explanation: `System.in` is an `InputStream` (bytes). `BufferedReader` needs a `Reader`, so wrap it in the bridge class `InputStreamReader`. `FileReader` takes a file, not a stream.

lessons.title: Serialization
lessons.summary: Turning objects into bytes and back.

blocks.text: **Serialization** writes an object (and everything it references) as bytes. **Deserialization** rebuilds it. A class opts in by implementing `java.io.Serializable`, a **marker interface** with no methods.

items: `ObjectOutputStream.writeObject(obj)` writes it.
`ObjectInputStream.readObject()` returns **`Object`**, so you must **cast**. It throws `IOException` and the checked `ClassNotFoundException`.
`serialVersionUID` is a version number. If the stored value differs from the class's current one, reading throws `InvalidClassException`.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Like `pickle`, but Java refuses classes that didn't opt in: writing a non-`Serializable` object throws `NotSerializableException`.

blocks.title: No cast, no compile
blocks.text: `Cat c = in.readObject();` does not compile: the return type is `Object`. A wrong cast compiles but throws `ClassCastException` at runtime.

steps.prompt: Complete the code that saves and restores a `Cat`.
steps.explanation: `ObjectOutputStream.writeObject` saves the object. `readObject()` returns `Object`, so it must be cast to `(Cat)`. `write` only writes bytes.

items: **`transient`** fields are skipped on purpose (passwords, caches).
**`static`** fields belong to the class, not the object, so they are never saved.
On deserialization, the Serializable class's **constructors and field initializers do not run**. Skipped fields get default values: `0`, `false`, `null`.

blocks.title: Initializers don't help
blocks.text: `transient int tries = 3;` comes back as **0**, not 3: the initializer isn't run during deserialization. And a `static` field shows whatever value the class has **now**, not when the object was saved.

steps.explanation: `name` is saved. `tries` and `pin` are transient, so they come back as `0` and `null`; the initializers don't run. `count` is static: not saved, and it was changed to 9 before reading, so 9 is printed.

blocks.text: When an object is deserialized, Java walks up its class hierarchy to the **first superclass that is not Serializable** and runs **that class's no-arg constructor**. Serializable classes below it get no constructor call; their fields come from the stream.

blocks.title: No accessible no-arg constructor
blocks.text: If that first non-serializable superclass has no accessible no-arg constructor, the code still **compiles**, but deserialization fails at runtime with `InvalidClassException`.

steps.explanation: `new Dog()` prints `A` then `D`. Deserializing runs only the no-arg constructor of the first non-serializable superclass, `Animal`: one more `A`. `Dog()` is not called. Total: `ADA`.

blocks.text: Serialization saves the whole object graph. Every non-transient, non-static field must hold something serializable (or `null`). Otherwise `writeObject` throws **`NotSerializableException`** at runtime.

blocks.title: Mostly safe
blocks.text: `String`, wrapper classes like `Integer`, arrays of serializable things, and the common collections (`ArrayList`, `HashMap`) are all serializable.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: It compiles: the compiler doesn't check field types. At runtime `writeObject` reaches the `Engine` object, which isn't `Serializable`, and throws `NotSerializableException` before `saved` is printed.

items: A **record** that implements `Serializable` is rebuilt by calling its **canonical constructor**, so validation in a compact constructor runs again.
There's no "-1" or "null" at the end of an object stream: `readObject()` throws **`EOFException`** when no object is left. Catch it to end a read loop.

blocks.caption: Reading until the end of the stream

steps.explanation: The compact constructor runs when the record is created (`R`). Records are deserialized through their canonical constructor, so it runs a second time when the copy is read: `RR`.

steps.prompt: `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` returns `null` when it reaches the end of the stream.
steps.explanation: It throws `EOFException`. `null` can't mean "end" because `null` is a valid value that may have been written with `writeObject(null)`.

steps.prompt: Which two field values are NOT written by `writeObject`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `transient` fields are skipped on purpose, and `static` fields belong to the class, not the instance. `private`, `final` and array fields are all saved normally.

blocks.text: NIO.2 (`java.nio.file`) represents a location with the **`Path`** interface. Create one with `Path.of(...)` or the older `Paths.get(...)`; both do the same thing.

blocks.caption: Parts are joined with the separator

items: **Absolute** paths start at the root (`/` on Unix, `C:\\` on Windows). Everything else is **relative** to the current directory.
Creating a `Path` does **not** touch the file system. The file doesn't have to exist.
`Path` is **immutable**: methods return a new `Path`.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Similar to `pathlib.Path`. But Java uses `Path.of(...)` (no `new`, it's an interface) and joins with `resolve`, not `/`.

blocks.code:
Path p =
    Path.of("/zoo/animals/bear/koala.txt");
p.getFileName()  // koala.txt
p.getParent()    // /zoo/animals/bear
p.getRoot()      // /
p.getNameCount() // 4
p.getName(0)     // zoo
p.subpath(1, 3)  // animals/bear

items: The root is **not** a name. `getName(0)` is the element closest to the root.
`subpath(begin, end)`: `end` is **exclusive**, like `substring`. Bad indexes throw `IllegalArgumentException`.
`getParent()` and `getRoot()` return **null** when there's nothing to return, e.g. `Path.of("koala.txt").getParent()`.

blocks.title: Index errors
blocks.text: `subpath(0, 5)` on a 4-name path throws `IllegalArgumentException`, not `IndexOutOfBoundsException`. So does `getName(4)`.

blocks.title: Names, not characters
blocks.text: `Path.startsWith` and `endsWith` compare **whole name elements**, unlike `String`. `Path.of("/data").startsWith("/da")` is `false`. A root-only path has no names: `Path.of("/").getFileName()` is `null` and `getNameCount()` is 0.

steps.explanation: The root `/` isn't counted, so there are 4 names: zoo(0), animals(1), bear(2), koala.txt(3). `subpath(1, 3)` takes indexes 1 and 2: `animals/bear`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: A relative path with one name has no parent and no root, so both methods return `null`. No exception is thrown.

blocks.text: `p.resolve(q)` joins `q` onto `p`. If `q` is **absolute**, the result is just `q`.

blocks.caption: Absolute argument wins

blocks.text: `p.resolveSibling(q)` resolves `q` against `p`'s **parent**: handy for a file next to `p`. An absolute `q` is again returned as is.
`p.relativize(q)` answers: how do I get from `p` to `q`? Both must be absolute, or both relative; mixing them throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

blocks.caption: Walk up with .., then down

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: From `a/b`, go up one level to `a`, then down into `c/x`: `../c/x`. Both paths are relative, so relativize is allowed.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that throws an exception at runtime.
steps.explanation: `p3` is `/data/logs/app.log` and `p4` is the relative `data/logs`. Line 5 relativizes a relative path against an absolute one, which throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

items: `normalize()` removes `.` and resolves `x/..` pairs, purely as text. Leading `..` in a relative path stays.
`toAbsolutePath()` puts the current directory in front of a relative path. No file needs to exist.
`toRealPath()` asks the file system: it normalizes, follows symbolic links, and throws **`NoSuchFileException`** (an `IOException`) if the file doesn't exist.

blocks.title: Immutable: the ignored return value
blocks.text: `p.normalize();` on its own line does nothing useful: `p` is unchanged and the new `Path` is thrown away. Exam code loves this. Write `p = p.normalize();`.

steps.explanation: `normalize()` returns a **new** Path and `p` is never reassigned. Printing `p` shows the original text.

blocks.text: `Path.equals` compares the path **text** (no normalizing, no file system). `Files.isSameFile(a, b)` asks the file system whether both point to the same file.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: `Files.isSameFile` returns `true` immediately if the paths are `equals`. Otherwise it really looks at the files on disk, so it declares `throws IOException`.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: `Path.of("data.txt")` throws an exception if the file doesn't exist.
`normalize()` modifies the Path it is called on.
`relativize` works between an absolute and a relative path.
steps.explanation: `resolve` returns its argument when the argument is absolute. `toRealPath` reads the file system and throws `NoSuchFileException` for missing files. Creating a Path never checks existence, `Path` is immutable, and mixing absolute/relative in `relativize` throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

lessons.title: Files basics
lessons.summary: Check, create, delete, copy and move.

blocks.text: `java.nio.file.Files` is a class of **static** methods that act on `Path`s. Most of them throw the checked **`IOException`** (or a subclass).

blocks.title: Exceptions you'll see
blocks.text: All in `java.nio.file`, all subclasses of `IOException`: `NoSuchFileException`, `FileAlreadyExistsException`, `DirectoryNotEmptyException`.

`exists`, `isRegularFile` and `isDirectory` **follow symbolic links**: they look at the target. Pass `LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS` to check the link itself. `Files.isSymbolicLink(p)` asks whether `p` is a link.

blocks.caption: A link to a file that doesn't exist

items: `createFile(p)`: new empty file. Throws `FileAlreadyExistsException` if it exists.
`createDirectory(p)`: one directory. The **parent must exist** (else `NoSuchFileException`); throws `FileAlreadyExistsException` if it exists.
`createDirectories(p)`: creates all missing parents too, and does **nothing** if the directory already exists.

blocks.caption: Calling createDirectories twice is fine

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `createDirectory` creates exactly one level. The parent `x` doesn't exist, so it throws `NoSuchFileException`. `createDirectories` would have worked.

items: `delete(p)` throws `NoSuchFileException` if nothing is there.
`deleteIfExists(p)` returns `true` if it deleted something, `false` if nothing was there.
Both throw **`DirectoryNotEmptyException`** for a directory that still has entries. There's no built-in recursive delete.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `deleteIfExists` only avoids the exception for a **missing** path. The directory exists and contains `n.txt`, so it throws `DirectoryNotEmptyException`.

blocks.text: `Files.copy(source, target, options...)` and `Files.move(source, target, options...)`. By default they **refuse to overwrite**: if the target exists they throw `FileAlreadyExistsException`.

rows: `move` happens as one step, or fails with `AtomicMoveNotSupportedException`

items: Copying a **directory** copies only the directory itself, not its contents (a shallow copy).
`move` renames when source and target are in the same directory.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `shutil.copy` silently overwrites. Java's `Files.copy` throws unless you pass `REPLACE_EXISTING`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `b.txt` already exists and no `REPLACE_EXISTING` option is given, so `move` throws `FileAlreadyExistsException`.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so that the copy overwrites `backup.txt` if it already exists.
steps.code:
Files.___(src, dst,
    StandardCopyOption.___);
steps.explanation: `Files.copy` with `StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING` overwrites the target. `ATOMIC_MOVE` is for `move`, and there is no `OVERWRITE` option.
`hello` is 5 bytes. The file is a regular file, so `isRegularFile` is true and `isDirectory` is false.

steps.prompt: `Files.createDirectories(p)` throws `FileAlreadyExistsException` when the directory `p` already exists.
steps.explanation: `createDirectories` succeeds quietly if the directory is already there. Only `createDirectory` (singular) throws in that case. (Both throw if `p` exists as a regular file.)

lessons.title: Reading, writing & walking with Files
lessons.summary: readAllLines vs lines, list, walk and find.

blocks.text: All use UTF-8 by default. Writing **creates or overwrites** the file unless you pass `StandardOpenOption.APPEND`.
`Files.lines` keeps the file open while the stream is used. Close the stream, ideally with try-with-resources.

blocks.title: Big files
blocks.text: `readAllLines` loads everything at once and can run out of memory on a huge file. `lines` reads as the stream asks for data. Note the types: `List<String>` vs `Stream<String>`.

steps.explanation: `Files.lines` returns `Stream<String>`; `Files.readAllLines` returns `List<String>`. The other combinations don't compile.

steps.prompt: Put the lines in order to print each line of `f` in upper case and close the file.
steps.explanation: Open the stream as a resource in `try (...)`, chain the operations, and the closing brace closes the file.

items: All three return a `Stream<Path>` that must be **closed**.
`find` needs a `maxDepth` (no overload without it) and a `BiPredicate<Path, BasicFileAttributes>`.
Symbolic links are not followed unless you pass `FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS`.

blocks.caption: list: a.txt, sub. walk adds the start and sub/b.txt

steps.explanation: `walk` includes the start directory itself. Depth 1 adds its direct children `x.txt` and `in`. `in/y.txt` is at depth 2, beyond the limit. Total: **3**.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that causes a compilation error.
steps.explanation: `Files.find` has no overload without the `int maxDepth` argument. It must be `Files.find(d, 10, (p, a) -> ...)`. `Files.list` with one argument is fine.

blocks.text: `Files.readAttributes(path, BasicFileAttributes.class)` reads several attributes in one call. `BasicFileAttributes` lives in `java.nio.file.attribute`.

items: Also: `creationTime()`, `lastModifiedTime()`, `lastAccessTime()` (all `FileTime`), `isSymbolicLink()`.
To **change** timestamps, use `Files.getFileAttributeView(p, BasicFileAttributeView.class).setTimes(...)` or `Files.setLastModifiedTime`.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: `Files.list` returns only the direct entries of a directory.
The stream returned by `Files.walk` should be closed.
`Files.writeString` appends to an existing file by default.
steps.explanation: `list` is one level deep, and all of `list`, `walk`, `find` and `lines` hold the file system open, so close them. `walk` does include the start path, `readAllLines` returns a `List`, and `writeString` truncates unless you pass `APPEND`.
Without `StandardOpenOption.APPEND`, `writeString` uses `CREATE`, `TRUNCATE_EXISTING` and `WRITE`: the second call replaces the content.

lessons.title: Old vs new: File vs Path
lessons.summary: Mapping java.io.File to Path and Files.

blocks.text: `java.io.File` is the original (Java 1.0) way to point at a file. NIO.2's `Path` + `Files` replaced it, but the exam still expects you to map between them.

blocks.caption: Converting between the two

blocks.title: Biggest difference
blocks.text: `File` methods usually report failure by returning **`false`** (or `null`). `Files` methods throw an **exception** that says why.

blocks.title: Name traps
blocks.text: There's no `Files.isFile` and no `File.isRegularFile`. `getName()` is `File`; `getFileName()` is `Path`.

steps.explanation: `mkdirs()` creates missing parents, like `Files.createDirectories`. `createDirectory` matches `mkdir()`. `Files.mkdirs` and `Path.mkdirs` don't exist.

blocks.caption: File just says false, without a reason

items: `File.listFiles()` returns `null` (not an empty array) when the `File` isn't a directory.
`File.length()` returns `0` for a file that doesn't exist.
With NIO.2 the exception type tells you what went wrong.

options: false, then an exception is thrown
true, then an exception is thrown
steps.explanation: `File.delete()` returns `false` when there is nothing to delete. `Files.delete` throws `NoSuchFileException` instead.

steps.prompt: `new File("report.txt")` creates an empty file named report.txt on disk.
steps.explanation: Like `Path.of`, the constructor only creates an object that describes a location. Use `createNewFile()` or `Files.createFile` to actually create the file.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The file doesn't exist. `exists()` returns `false`, `length()` returns `0`, and `listFiles()` returns `null` for anything that isn't a directory. `File` methods don't throw here.

steps.prompt: Complete the NIO.2 versions of the `File` calls in the comments.
steps.explanation: `isFile` → `Files.isRegularFile`, `getName` → `Path.getFileName`, `length` → `Files.size`. `Path` does have a `getName(int)`, but it needs an index, and `Files` has no `isFile` or `length`.

steps.prompt: Which two return types are correct? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `File.getParent()` is a `String` (use `getParentFile()` for a `File`), while `Path.getParent()` is a `Path`. `File.lastModified()` is a `long` of milliseconds; NIO.2 uses `FileTime`. `Files.list` returns `Stream<Path>`.

lessons.title: Unit 9 checkpoint
lessons.summary: Exam-style mix: streams, serialization, Path, Files.

blocks.text: 12 exam-style questions covering the whole unit. Read each line carefully: one constructor type, one missing option or one ignored return value changes the answer.

blocks.title: Exam habit
blocks.text: First ask: does it compile? (Stream families mixed, `readObject` without a cast, `find` without `maxDepth`.) Then: does it throw? (Existing target without `REPLACE_EXISTING`, non-empty directory, mixed absolute/relative `relativize`.)

steps.explanation: `resolve` returns its argument when the argument is absolute, so the result is `/c/d`. `normalize` doesn't change it.

`System.out` is a byte stream; `OutputStreamWriter` bridges it to a `Writer`, which `BufferedWriter` accepts. `BufferedWriter`/`BufferedReader` can't take byte streams directly, and `InputStreamReader` wants an `InputStream`, not a `Reader`.
`name` is saved. `level` and `active` are transient, so they come back with defaults `0` and `false`. Field initializers of a Serializable class don't run during deserialization.
Creating `Q` runs `P()` then `Q()`: `PQ`. On deserialization only the no-arg constructor of the first non-serializable superclass (`P`) runs: `P`. Result: `PQP`.

steps.explanation: `readPassword` returns `char[]` so it can be wiped. `readLine` ends with `null`, `read` with `-1`. Print methods never throw `IOException`, and `System.in` is an `InputStream`, not a `Reader`.
`equals` compares the text: `x/../q.txt` is not `q.txt`, so `false`. `isSameFile` asks the file system, which resolves `x/..` and finds the same file: `true`.

The `FileWriter` is never flushed or closed before `Files.size`, so the file is still empty: 0. Then the try-with-resources `PrintWriter` writes `x` and closes, which **overwrites** the file (no append flag): `x`.
From `/a/b/c`, two steps up reach `/a`, then down into `x/y`: `../../x/y`.
